identity.title: Dustin Crummett vs Ben Watkins: Does the Soul Exist?
identity.label: Soul and mind–body identity

routes.speaker: Dustin Crummett

bridges.statement: Persons exist as simple, indivisible, immaterial subjects of experience.
The determinate unity and persistence of a conscious subject cannot be identified with a divisible material object.
Mental-physical correlations are contingent psychophysical laws rather than necessary supervenience relations.
Substance dualism accommodates mental causation, conceivability evidence, and personal identity with less unexplained necessity.

routes.position: The soul exists as a nonphysical aspect of persons

routes.speaker: Ben Watkins

bridges.statement: The case for a nonphysical soul is unsuccessful.
Mental changes and capacities depend upon physical brains through sufficient physical causes and necessary supervenience.
Personal persistence is reducible to psychological connectedness rather than an enduring immaterial subject.
Causal closure and conservation of energy count against interaction between physical bodies and nonphysical souls.

routes.position: The case for a nonphysical soul is unsuccessful

sections.title: Mind–Body Foundations and Rival Ontologies
sections.rationale: Establishes the shared hard problem, the rival monist and dualist frameworks, and Crummett's target conception of persons.

moves.speaker: Ben Watkins
moves.excerpt: is that minds are real and irreducible. If it consciously seems like we are conscious, then there is consciousness. Because appearance and reality coincide here, the distinction between them disappears. So there is a hard problem of consciousness. Minds are neither identical nor reducible to brains. The second place I want to start is that minds causally interact with the body. We drink water because we are thirsty. The conscious mental state of being thirsty is what causes the body to drink water. So there's good reason to believe there is some solution to the interaction problem. moves.speaker: Ben Watkins
moves.excerpt: Thank you. Um I these are some anti- reductionist anti-reductionist options that we can put on the table because um that's where I find myself these days. I find myself firmly in the anti-productionist camp. Um so there's the view dual aspect monism that insists there's a single re uh irreducible substance but it is describable in both physical and mental terms. Uh there's property dualism which denies there are two unique substances but insists there are two unique properties in the universe and then epiphenomenalism which conceds minds are a non-physical substance ben denies that minds and brains causally interact. Now I've listed all three of these and it might seem that I think all three of these are on a par but that's not so. Um it's time to whiff uh sift and winnow so to speak. Um, epiphenomenalism already is in tension with one of the things we wanted to conceive. We wanted to in our original mindbody problem to concede that minds causally interact with the body. So we can take epifenomenalism off the table and we're left with this dual aspect monism or a or a form of property dualism. So, um, what do we want to choose? Well, I don't know if I can decide that question today because I haven't decided it myself. I lean more towards dual aspect monism at the current moment. Um and so um that view is going to deny that the mental and the physical are distinct substances. But it's instead going to claim that the mental and physical concepts are two inseparable and mutually irreducible perspectives or aspects of a single substance. This view avoids both the interaction problem and the pairing problem while also insisting the mind and the body are real and irreducible to one another.

moves.proposition: Dual-aspect monism offers one substance under mutually irreducible mental and physical perspectives, preserving consciousness while avoiding substance-dualist interaction and pairing problems.

sections.title: Transplants, Fission, and Personal Identity
sections.rationale: Contains the principal affirmative transplant argument and Watkins's direct reductionist treatment of fission.

moves.speaker: Dustin Crummett
moves.excerpt: Um so to begin the argument, consider the fact that sometimes people have what are called hemispherectomies. Uh so you can have a hemisphere of your brain removed for medical reasons, usually has to do with seizures, I think. Uh it turns out that enough stuff is duplicated between the two hemispheres of your brain uh that you can actually have this done and not change very much. keep your personality, keep your memories, be able to do the same stuff, etc. Uh, this is this is empirically true. Yeah. So, so when you just some clear Okay, you have a slide up here. So, they they take out literally like half of the brain. Mhm. Wow. Yeah. They they remove a hemisphere of your brain uh and leave you with one one hemisphere. Um so uh it seems to me uh that I can survive a successful hemispherectomy not just in the sense that my pulse continues or whatever but in the sense that the subject of experience before will be the same as the subject of experience after the surgery. Um if for whatever reason you're skeptical about that it will be enough for my purposes if we agree that it's metaphysically possible. If we have to get into that, I'll explain why. It's enough for my purposes, but I'll talk as if these judgments are about actual cases. So, here's a second case. Uh, I call this single transplant. So, suppose I have a hemispherectomy. One of my hemispheres is removed and it is destroyed. Thrown in with the medical waste. Uh, sometime later, my body is failing. The scientists decide best way to save me is to uh transplant uh my remaining hemisphere into a new body. my old body dies. Now, if I survived the hemispherectomy, it seems to me that I ought to be able to survive this too in the sense of maintaining continuity of subject. Right? Uh my brain is the thing that is the causal basis of my experiences, my thoughts, my memories, etc. So, I will go with my brain. I will be the subject of the experiences that the person in the new body is having, right? The person in the new body will be me. um or at least that's metaphysically possible. Now consider uh a slight variation called single transplant no weight. This is the same as the last case except both operations happen at the same time. So the doctors take out both hemispheres, they destroy one at the same time they transplant the other one. Um so this is just the same as single transplant except we don't wait. Uh, and I think that if I could survive in single transplant, I ought to be able to survive here, too. Why would waiting to do the transplant make any difference, much less make it metaphysically impossible, right? Uh, but consider yet another variant called double transplant. Uh, here they uh again remove both hemispheres of my brain at the same time, but instead of destroying one, they transplant both of them into new bodies. We can even add that these are clone bodies that are identical to my original body. Right? So, we put the left hemisphere of my brain into [clears throat] a new body and we call that person Mr. Left. We put the right hemisphere simultaneously into a new body and we call that person Mr. Right. Now, uh Mr. Left and Mr. Right are both physically and psychologically continuous with me before the surgery. The person who was there before the surgery, right? Um, in fact, we can even make it so that they're identical if we want. Uh, that would be unrealistic, but we could make it that way. Um, further, they both have the same kind of causal connection to the original person, right? Uh, but it's clear that they're not both me. Uh, they can't both be me because they are not Mr. Left is not the same person as Mr. Right. And so, they can't be numerically identical to me because numerical identity is transitive, right? So, if Mr. Left is not Mr. Right? Then I can't be both of them. Right? So either I am Mr. Left and Mr. Right as a new person or I am Mr. Right and Mr. Left is a new person or I am not having any experiences at all anymore and they are both new people. So the question is will I be having one of these people's sets of experiences when uh the surgery ends or will I not have any more experiences?
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the subject of experience before will be the same
moves.proposition: Survival through hemispherectomy and single transplant is possible, but symmetrical double transplantation cannot yield two numerically identical continuers, creating a determinate fission trilemma for material identity.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is the core thought experiment from which the affirmative case develops.

sections.title: Mental Causation and Physical Closure
sections.rationale: Covers conservation of energy, basic causation, and whether the objection applies equally to anti-reductionist monism.

moves.speaker: Ben Watkins
moves.excerpt: consciousness and personality are correlated with a sufficient physical cause. We could infer from this fact that all changes in mental properties probably have a sufficient physical cause. Such an inference would be as strong as the inference that the next vertebrae we encounter will have a brain because all previously observed vertebrae have been correlated with having a brain. Now admittedly an an inductive sampling um is biased against unobserved causes. Um so that's why I have more than one claim. Um the second claim was that there are no mental differences without a physical difference. And so why do I believe that? Um I believe that because of what's called the causal closure of the physical. And so the causal closure of the physical claims that um primapasi non-physical events that causally interact with the physical world must be physically dependent. Otherwise we could not understand how they have any physical effects. Um the conservation of energy is a fundamental law of nature. Um that's uh the familiar um law of thermodynamics. Energy can be neither created nor destroyed. Rather, it can only change from one form to another. And the net total energy in an isolated system always remains constant over time. This is an empirical observation of the world. And so the energy from physical brains cannot causally interact with non-physical minds to reduce the net total of its own energy and vice versa. According to the interaction problem, physical and non-physical things cannot causally causally interact without implausibly deviating from a law of nature. Similar claims would apply to abstract objects because neither abstract objects have mass, energy or [clears throat] spatial extension. So that's why we consider abstract objects causally um inert. Um so using a simple likelihood evaluation we can say that um the conser conservation of energy um makes it more likely that there are no mental differences without a physical difference and less likely there are any non-physical minds. Um and then the last claim I made um is an inference to the best explanation. Um because it might be objected here that the laws of nature do not apply to non-physical minds or that our um

moves.proposition: Induction supports sufficient physical causes for mental changes, while causal closure and energy conservation make nonphysical causal intervention unlikely.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Watkins's principal empirical interaction argument.
